A: Chapter 16 (Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna) sets out the two endowments (sampad) with which beings are born. 16.1-3: the twenty-six marks of the divine endowment (fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in jñānayoga, giving, self-restraint, sacrifice, recitation, austerity, straightforwardness, non-harming, truth … absence of excessive pride). 16.4: the marks of the demonic endowment (hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, ignorance). 16.5: the divine leads to release, the demonic to bondage; Arjuna is told not to grieve, being born to the divine. 16.6: there are two creations of beings, divine and demonic; the demonic is now described at length. 16.7-18: the demonic know neither engagement nor withdrawal and have no purity, conduct or truth; they hold the world to be without truth, foundation or Lord and caused by desire (16.8); they come forth for the world's destruction, driven by insatiable desire, endless cares and unjust gain (16.9-12); their self-conceit is voiced in their own words (16.13-15) and they fall into hell (16.16); they sacrifice in name only and hate the Lord in their own and others' bodies (16.17-18). 16.19-20: the Lord casts them into demonic wombs, and they sink lower birth after birth without reaching him. 16.21-22: desire, anger and greed are the threefold gate of hell, to be abandoned; the one freed from them does what is good for the self and reaches the highest course. 16.23-24: whoever abandons the injunction of scripture for desire gains neither perfection, happiness nor the highest course; scripture is therefore Arjuna's authority on what is to be done and not done, and he should act knowing it.

the impulses and constituents of action (18.18). 18.19-40: knowledge, action, agent, understanding, steadiness and happiness, each threefold by the guṇas; no being is free of the guṇas (18.40). 18.41-48: the works of the four varṇas born of their nature; A: The verse does not say which dharmas are to be abandoned or in what sense. Commentators divide sharply: abandoning all dharma and adharma, i.e. all action, for knowledge (Śaṅkara); giving up the other means (or taking refuge in their place) and relying on the Lord alone (Rāmānuja; the Śrīvaiṣṇava 'carama-śloka'); giving up the sense of agency and attachment while still doing one's duties (other readings). 'mokṣayiṣyāmi' is 'I will release', its object being 'from all sins'. 'mā śucaḥ' echoes 16.5 and answers the grief of 1.47-2.11. Called 'the most secret of all' by 18.64.
B: 'mā śucaḥ' closes the teaching that began with 'you grieve for those not to be grieved for' (2.11); 'śaraṇaṃ vraja' answers Arjuna's 'tvāṃ prapannam' (2.7), and 'all dharmas' his 'dharma-saṃmūḍha-cetāḥ' (2.7). The commentators divide sharply on 'sarva-dharmān parityajya': renouncing all actions, dharma and adharma alike, in favour of knowledge of the one self (Śaṅkara); giving up the sense of agency, possession and fruit in all dharmas, or — for one unable to begin bhakti-yoga — surrender in place of the expiations and yogas (Rāmānuja); in the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition the verse is the carama-śloka (trm:carama-sloka), the charter of prapatti. The paraphrase keeps the verse's own words.
resolution: The verse does not say which dharmas are to be abandoned or in what sense (A). 'mā śucaḥ' closes the teaching that began with 'you grieve for those not to be grieved for' (2.11) and echoes 16.5; 'śaraṇaṃ vraja' answers Arjuna's 'tvāṃ prapannam' (2.7), and 'all dharmas' his 'dharma-saṃmūḍha-cetāḥ' (2.7) (B). 18.64 marks this word, with 18.65, as 'the most secret of all'. 'mokṣayiṣyāmi' is 'I will release', its object being 'from all sins'. The commentators divide sharply on 'sarva-dharmān parityajya': renouncing all actions, dharma and adharma alike, in favour of knowledge of the one self (Śaṅkara); giving up the sense of agency, possession and fruit in all dharmas, or — for one unable to begin bhakti-yoga — taking refuge in place of the other means and expiations (Rāmānuja); giving up the sense of agency and attachment while still doing one's duties (other readings). In the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition the verse is the carama-śloka (data/ trm:carama-sloka), the charter of prapatti. cpt:prapatti and trm:prapatti are deliberately not linked: the verse has no form of pra-√pad, and those data/ entries define the Śrīvaiṣṇava doctrine; the verse is linked in the Gītā's own terms (cpt:surrender-to-the-lord, prc:saranagati, trm:sarana, trm:saranagati) and to dsp:is-prapatti-an-upaya, whose Viśiṣṭādvaita side cites it.
